newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Ragged Australian bonds pare fall for now.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Ragged Australian bonds pare fall for now.

text.p: Australian bonds succumbed to another whippy session with long-dated yields particularly hit by the gyrations in U.S. Treasury and futures markets.

The benchmark 10-year bond yield spiked over 7.50 percent at one stage, and some 30 basis points from Tuesday's close, before the market bounced just after the release of the November labour force report.
"There were some heavy flows just before the figure, but where we go from here is anybody's guess," one trader said.
At face value the data was stronger than expected, but analysts did not see this as a turning point in the market.

Employment rose 24,400 and was near the top of the forecast range, although this was made up of 18,700 of part-time workers, while the unemployment rate fell to 8.5 percent compared to median 8.7 percent expectations.

John Peters, economist at Westpac, said the data did not change his view that labour market conditions remain fairly weak. He added that if retail demand remains soft and enterprise bargaining agreements contained, there could be another rate cut early next year.
The Reserve Bank made a surprise cut in official interest rates to 6.0 percent on Wednesday.

However, this has already become a distant memory for the long-end of the market which saw its rate cut rally completely wiped out in after hours trading as U.S. Treasuries saw heavy selling from overseas investors in New York.

Concerns following comments by U.S. investment house Goldman Sachs that Japanese investors could taper their demand for U.S. debt sent jitters through the market on Wednesday, but the market slightly pulled back in Tokyo trading.
However, there were rumours in Tokyo of massive selling of Canadian bonds by Japanese investors.

Local long bonds underperformed the rest of the dollar bloc, with Canada and New Zealand debt both taking their leads from the U.S.
The local yield curve extended Wednesday's steepening with the short-end protected by the surprise rate cut by the RBA.
